findings.description: The RDS instance sets publicly_accessible = true, giving it a public IP and exposing the MySQL endpoint to the internet rather than keeping it private within the VPC.
storage_encrypted = false means the database volume and snapshots are unencrypted, so anyone obtaining the underlying storage or a snapshot can read all customer data.

The master password is supplied from var.password directly into the resource and reused in EC2 user_data; the credential is stored in Terraform state in plaintext instead of using a secrets manager or manage_master_user_password.
The master username is the predictable default 'admin', making credential-stuffing and brute-force attacks against the publicly reachable database easier.

findings.issue_category: no TLS enforcement / no IAM auth
findings.description: The parameter group does not set require_secure_transport and iam_database_authentication_enabled is not enabled, so clients may connect to the internet-exposed MySQL instance over unencrypted channels with static passwords.
skip_final_snapshot = true combined with backup_retention_period = 0 means deletion of the instance (e.g. by an attacker with rds:* permissions) destroys all data with no recovery point.
The instance role grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*", so compromise of the web server yields near-full control of storage, compute and databases in the account.

The DB master username and password are interpolated into EC2 user_data, which is readable in plaintext via the instance metadata service (and by anyone with ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute), leaking database credentials.
No metadata_options block requiring http_tokens = "required", so IMDSv1 remains enabled; an SSRF against the PHP app could retrieve the highly privileged instance-profile credentials.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the instance's root volume (which stores the plaintext dbinfo.inc credentials file) may be unencrypted at rest.
The instance is launched in a public subnet and exports a public DNS output while serving an unauthenticated HTTP-only PHP page, providing an internet-facing attack surface with no TLS.
The database security group allows all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, enabling data exfiltration or command-and-control traffic from a compromised database host.
The attached ingress rule permits MySQL 3306 from the entire VPC CIDR rather than only the application security group, so any workload in the VPC can reach the database directly.
The database endpoint of a publicly accessible instance is exported as an unmarked Terraform output, aiding attacker reconnaissance of the internet-reachable DB.
